author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: An early novel (1957) in which a man returns to his Virginia hometown to find it subtly, impossibly altered—the ground on which two warring cosmic deities, Ormazd and Ahriman, fight to rewrite reality itself; PKD's first sustained treatment of the world as a false surface over a hidden true one.
page_summary:
Ted Barton drives back to the town where he grew up, Millgate, and discovers it is wrong: the streets, the buildings, even the records show a place he does not remember, and he learns that the boy he was is listed as having died in childhood. The town has been overwritten. Behind the alteration stand two ancient forces—the Zoroastrian creator Ormazd and the destroyer Ahriman—contending for control, with local children who can animate clay figures and a reality that can be dissolved and remade by will.

This is PKD's most explicitly dualist early book: the experienced world is a screen, and the true world lies concealed beneath it, accessible only once the deception is perceived. The accumulation of small wrong details—a building that should be there and isn't, a memory that no longer matches the record—becomes his lifelong method for staging reality breakdown, here given a frankly theological engine. Restoring the town means restoring the real beneath the counterfeit.

Developed from an earlier magazine version ('A Glass of Darkness'), the novel is minor as narrative but load-bearing as seed. Its Manichean structure—a good creator locked out, a hidden real world, salvation as recognition—anticipates the gnostic framework PKD would spend his last decade elaborating in the Exegesis and the VALIS books.
